note: Declarative export fixtures. Both implementations build identical inputs from this file: the legacy Python exporters (tools/generate_golden.py, which writes goldens/) and the TypeScript library under test. Rects are [x1, y1, x2, y2] with x2/y2 EXCLUSIVE, matching numpy slicing. Vertices are [x, y] in pixels. imageSize is [height, width], as the legacy ExportContext stores it.

cases.why: Non-contiguous per-image class ids (3, 7) must be written verbatim, never renumbered 0..N-1 (RULE-005).
One segment whose pixels fall in two islands writes two lines, in OpenCV contour order rather than top-to-bottom (RULE-005).
A mask touching all four edges makes normalized width and height exactly 1.0, which Python writes as '1.0' and naive JavaScript as '1' (RULE-005).
A single pixel on an 8192px image drives coordinates below 1e-4, where Python switches to exponential form with a zero-padded exponent (RULE-005).
Python's json.dump escapes non-ASCII as \uXXXX by default; JSON.stringify does not (RULE-001).
Overlapping classes stay set in both channels when pixel priority is off (RULE-014).
With pixel priority ascending the lowest class wins the overlap, which changes masks, boxes and polygons.
Descending priority hands the overlap to the highest class instead.
Polygon and circle segments are rasterized at save time: vertices truncate toward zero and the circle radius rounds half-to-even (RULE-016 and the shape rasterization rule).
The crop end coordinates are clamped inclusively but sliced exclusively, so the image's last row and column can never survive a crop (RULE-016).
NPZ Class Map stores class 0 and needs the foreground mask to tell it apart from background (RULE-003).
A one-pixel object has an inclusive bounding span of 1 and a contour of a single point, which the polygon formats must still handle.
